analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from owning both a pharmacy and a pharmacy benefit manager or insurer.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2026 with two Republican and one Democratic cosponsor, the bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: Six pharmacy benefit managers, all owned by or tied to giant health conglomerates, handle the vast majority of American prescriptions. Because the companies that decide what your drugs cost often also own the pharmacies that sell them, they can steer your business to their own stores. This bill would force any company that owns an insurer or a pharmacy benefit manager to sell off its pharmacies within a year, and gives federal agencies, state attorneys general, and ordinary citizens the power to enforce that split in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay more at the counter when their prescriptions are steered to a PBM's own stores, independent pharmacies that have been squeezed by unfair contracts, and taxpayers, since the bill's findings argue companies hide insurance profits inside unregulated pharmacy arms. People who were overcharged at vertically integrated pharmacies could share in court-ordered disgorgement funds.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any person to own a pharmacy while also owning an insurance company or a pharmacy benefit manager, and requires violators to divest the pharmacy within one year of enactment.

Lets the FTC and the Justice Department's antitrust division enforce the split, escrow 10% of a noncompliant company's profits each month until it divests, and appoint a trustee to sell the pharmacy if the company still refuses.

Gives state attorneys general and private individuals the right to sue, with treble damages and attorney's fees available to winning plaintiffs, and requires money disgorged from illegal pharmacy revenue to be distributed for the benefit of communities, including consumers overcharged at vertically integrated pharmacies.
Requires divestitures to be reported to the FTC and DOJ for antitrust review and lets those agencies block future deals that would re-create the same conflicts of interest.

The bill's findings cite FTC work showing vertically integrated PBMs steer business to their own affiliated pharmacies, raising drug costs, and point to the closure of more than 7,000 pharmacies between 2019 and 2024.

analysis.who_pays: The large health conglomerates that own pharmacy benefit managers and pharmacies — companies like CVS, Cigna, and UnitedHealth — would have to sell off their pharmacy businesses, and their shareholders would bear the cost of a forced breakup. Consumers could face some short-term disruption as pharmacy networks are rebuilt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Vertically integrated drug and insurance conglomerates

drawbacks.text: The one-year divestiture deadline is aggressive; a rushed breakup of pharmacy businesses this large risks short-term disruption to patients' access and pharmacy networks while the companies reorganize.

The bill attacks ownership conflicts but does not directly regulate how pharmacy benefit managers set prices or handle rebates, so drug prices would not necessarily fall immediately even if the breakups happen.
Enforcement depends on FTC and DOJ actions, rulemaking, and litigation, all of which take time and could be tied up in court challenges to the forced divestitures.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that the company negotiating your drug prices should not also own the store that sells them — addresses a conflict the FTC itself has flagged, and the enforcement tools are unusually strong. The real risks are execution: a one-year forced breakup of businesses this large could be chaotic, and because the bill leaves the rebate and pricing system alone, patients may wait a long time to see lower prices even if it were enacted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2026 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and nothing has happened to it since.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on May 13, 2026, joined by original cosponsors Senators Hawley, Fetterman, and Marshall, making the sponsorship bipartisan from the start.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, which is the only action recorded since introduction.

The bill's findings state that the six largest pharmacy benefit managers, each tied to a large health conglomerate, processed more than 90% of U.S. prescriptions in 2023, and that more than 7,000 pharmacies closed between 2019 and 2024.
As of the latest action history, the bill has not received a hearing, a markup, or any floor vote in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the vertically integrated pharmacy conglomerates: the bill has not moved, and the ownership structure it targets remains in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big vertically integrated pharmacy conglomerates, for now

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to force structural separation of pharmacies from pharmacy benefit managers and insurers.

for.name: Sens. Josh Hawley and Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Sen. John Fetterman
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent companies (CVS Health, Cigna, UnitedHealth)
against.role: Large health conglomerates that own the major PBMs and pharmacies
against.what_they_did: Have publicly fought PBM reform, and a nearly identical House bill was stripped from a December 2024 government funding package before it could get a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four sponsors split two Republicans and two Democrats, and there has been no roll-call or committee vote that would show whether that bipartisanship holds more broadly.

industries.industry: Vertically integrated health conglomerates (CVS Health, Cigna, UnitedHealth)
industries.note: They would be forced to sell their retail, mail-order, and specialty pharmacies within a year, undoing the structure that lets them steer prescriptions to their own stores and, per the bill's findings, hide insurance profits in unregulated pharmacy arms. Their gain under the current structure is ordinary patients' cost.

The bill's findings tie more than 7,000 pharmacy closures since 2019 partly to PBMs pressuring independent pharmacies into unfavorable contracts; removing the ownership conflict aims to restore competition from unaffiliated pharmacies.

industries.industry: PBM- and insurer-owned mail-order and specialty pharmacies
industries.note: These businesses exist largely because affiliated PBMs route prescriptions to them; divestiture would end that captive flow and put them on the open market.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Judiciary Committee with less than eight months left in the session. Most bills at this stage die without a hearing or a vote. The realistic path, if any, is attachment to a must-pass funding or health bill — the route a House version of this same idea took in late 2024 before being stripped from the package at the last minute.
